case_analysis.focal_point: Whether New Jersey Transit qualifies as an "arm of the State" entitled to interstate (constitutional) sovereign immunity, and how courts should weigh the State’s formal responsibility for judgments versus other arm-of-the-state factors.
case_analysis.legal_provision: State sovereign immunity doctrine under the U.S. Constitution (including the Eleventh Amendment framework as applied to interstate sovereign immunity), with related discussion of waiver principles (e.g., waiver/consent standards) and references to the New Jersey Tort Claims Act (N.J. Stat. Ann. §§ 59:1-1 to :12-3) as a claimed source of waiver.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioner (Galette) argues that New Jersey Transit should not be treated as an arm of the State for sovereign-immunity purposes—i.e., it functions more like a separate, state-created public enterprise than the State itself—so it can be sued in another State’s courts. Petitioner also attempts to point to New Jersey law (including the New Jersey Tort Claims Act’s treatment of certain ministerial acts) as supporting the view that immunity does not apply or has been waived in this context, and urges an arm-of-the-state analysis that does not let formal budgetary exposure alone control the outcome.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondent (New Jersey Transit/New Jersey) argues that NJ Transit is an arm of the State entitled to interstate sovereign immunity. It emphasizes that New Jersey’s legal structure makes the State financially responsible (or sufficiently exposed) for adverse judgments against NJ Transit, and contends that this liability factor should carry substantial—often dispositive—weight. Respondent also argues there is no valid waiver of constitutional sovereign immunity absent clear, express consent, rejecting any theory of constructive or implied waiver based on state tort-claims statutes or characterization of employee conduct as "ministerial."
key_precedents: Infinity Broad. Corp. v. N.J. Meadowlands Comm’n, 901 A.2d 312 (N.J. 2006)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Jackson’s and Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point is that NJ Transit’s corporate separateness and “sue-and-be-sued” clause signal functional independence, and that Hess does not expressly make treasury exposure dispositive. But Hess does identify the State’s legal and practical responsibility for satisfying judgments as the “most important factor,” and for a narrow, administrable rule tied to the core sovereignty concern—protecting the State’s fisc from out-of-state money judgments—that factor should control when the record shows substantial state backstopping. As Justice Kagan emphasizes, treating treasury exposure as merely coequal with open-ended functional considerations invites indeterminate balancing and unpredictability, especially where waiver is concededly absent under Edelman’s clear-statement principle. I would therefore affirm on the limited ground that New Jersey’s fiscal responsibility for NJ Transit’s judgments is sufficient here to treat it as an arm of the State, leaving harder separateness questions for a different statutory and evidentiary record.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson press the strongest counterargument: NJ Transit’s corporate separateness and “sue-and-be-sued” clause suggest operational independence, and Hess should not become a single-factor test. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Alito explain, Hess identifies the State treasury’s legal exposure as the “most important factor,” and on an originalist understanding of retained sovereign immunity, it is precisely the State’s fisc and dignity that the Constitution presupposes will not be subjected to sister-state damages judgments absent unmistakable consent. A general “sue-and-be-sued” authorization and the New Jersey Tort Claims Act fall well short of the clear waiver Edelman’s clear-statement rule demands for retroactive money liability, especially in another State’s courts. Functional autonomy cannot defeat immunity where state law and practical necessity place the State behind the entity’s judgments, because formalisms cannot be used to circumvent the structural immunity the Constitution assumes.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson press the best contrary point: NJ Transit’s corporate separateness and “sue-and-be-sued” clause, plus access-to-justice concerns, suggest we should treat it like a public enterprise rather than the State. But under Hess, the most important factor remains whether a money judgment will in law or unavoidable practical effect reach or meaningfully pressure the State treasury, and—as Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes—a rule anchored in fiscal exposure is more administrable than an open-ended functional balancing test. Their separateness argument also cannot do the work of a waiver: as Justice Kavanaugh and Justice Barrett note, neither the Tort Claims Act nor general “sue-and-be-sued” language supplies the unmistakably clear consent Edelman requires before allowing retrospective damages to be collected through a sister State’s courts. Even crediting operational autonomy, the constitutional immunity concern with protecting the State’s fisc and dignity is still directly implicated on this record, so I would adhere to respondent.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan are right that Hess calls state-treasury exposure the “most important factor,” and that point has real force because immunity’s structural purpose includes protecting the public fisc. But neither Hess nor our broader arm-of-the-State cases make treasury risk categorically dispositive where the State has deliberately created a separate corporate entity with “sue-and-be-sued” authority and meaningful operational autonomy; treating fiscal backstop risk as automatically controlling would, as Justice Jackson notes, collapse a multi-factor inquiry into a near-per se immunity rule. Justice Alito’s reliance on Edelman usefully reinforces the clear-statement rule against finding waiver, yet it does not resolve the antecedent question whether this entity is the State itself—especially where extending interstate immunity would predictably leave injured individuals without an effective forum against a public enterprise. On my pragmatic approach, functional separateness and the access-to-justice consequences remain weighty in the arm-of-the-State analysis even when the State may feel political or budgetary pressure to help cover judgments.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Jackson’s and Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point is that corporate separateness, operational autonomy, and a “sue-and-be-sued” clause should count heavily in the arm-of-the-State analysis, lest Hess devolve into a near-automatic immunity rule. But Hess’s designation of treasury exposure as the “most important factor,” reinforced by Justice Alito’s Edelman point about guarding against retrospective monetary liability absent unmistakable consent, counsels an administrable approach that treats meaningful state fiscal responsibility as near-dispositive when state law effectively puts the State behind the judgment. Chief Justice Roberts’s emphasis on avoiding indeterminate multi-factor balancing resonates with my pragmatic textualism: where waiver is absent and the consequence of the judgment predictably pressures the State fisc, functional independence cannot do the work petitioner needs. I therefore remain with Respondent on the narrow ground that this record shows sufficient State fiscal exposure to treat NJ Transit as an arm of New Jersey, without foreclosing different outcomes on materially different statutory funding structures.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Jackson’s caution against collapsing arm-of-the-State into a near-single-factor test deserves respect, but Hess’s identification of treasury exposure as the “most important factor” fits the original understanding that sovereign immunity principally protects a State’s fisc and corresponding political accountability from out-of-state damages judgments. Justice Sotomayor’s reliance on NJ Transit’s corporate form and “sue and be sued” clause cannot supply the unmistakably clear consent required to waive constitutional immunity in a sister State’s courts, and form cannot do the work of substance when state law makes New Jersey legally or effectively responsible for judgments. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan stress, anchoring the inquiry in legal fiscal responsibility avoids indeterminate balancing that invites inconsistent outcomes and interstate friction. Nothing raised in conference identifies a precedent that displaces Hess/Edelman’s clear-statement and fisc-protection framework on this record.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Jackson and Justice Sotomayor press the strongest counter: that NJ Transit’s corporate separateness, “sue-and-be-sued” clause, and enterprise-like operations counsel against treating it as the State, and they warn against collapsing the inquiry into a single factor that bars plaintiffs’ forum. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, Hess makes the State treasury’s legal/practical exposure the “most important factor,” and for an institutional, administrable doctrine in the interstate-immunity setting, that factor should be near-dispositive when state law effectively places the State behind the judgment. I also agree with Justice Barrett that neither the Tort Claims Act nor generic “sue-and-be-sued” language supplies the unmistakably clear waiver needed to subject a State (or its arm) to damages suits in a sister State’s courts. Because no colleague identifies a precedent displacing Hess’s treasury-risk primacy or relaxing our clear-statement waiver rule, I remain with Respondent.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson press the strongest contrary point: New Jersey chose a separate corporate form, gave NJ Transit "sue-and-be-sued" authority, and afforded operational autonomy, so immunity should not follow automatically from funding connections. But under Hess, as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize, the inquiry’s center of gravity is whether state law makes the State legally or functionally responsible for satisfying judgments, because that is what most directly implicates the Eleventh Amendment’s fiscal and dignity concerns in interstate litigation. On a textualist/originalist approach to retained sovereign immunity and our waiver cases, the "sue-and-be-sued" clause and the Tort Claims Act are not the unmistakably clear interstate-consent waiver Edelman requires, so corporate separateness cannot do the work of a waiver. I therefore would treat substantial state responsibility for judgments as near-dispositive on this record while leaving open that truly self-sustaining, non-backstopped entities might present a different case.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s administrability point—that Hess makes treasury exposure the “most important factor” and that near-dispositive weight yields a clearer rule—has force, but I do not think Hess (or Edelman) requires collapsing the arm-of-the-State inquiry into a single-factor test whenever an entity receives substantial state support. Edelman’s concern with retroactive money judgments reaching the State fisc is not fully triggered where state law creates a separate public corporation with “sue-and-be-sued” authority and purports to cabin the State’s legal obligation to pay, because the sovereignty/dignity rationale is materially weaker when the State has chosen separateness and operational independence. I agree with Justice Sotomayor (and with the respondents) that there is no unmistakable waiver in the Tort Claims Act, so the case turns on arm-of-the-State status; on this record, NJ Transit has not carried its burden to show the kind of legal (not just practical/political) treasury liability that should override its statutory separateness. Treating practical fiscal “pressure” as dispositive would predictably immunize a wide range of state-created enterprises and foreclose any forum for injured plaintiffs, a consequence I cannot justify under our multi-factor precedents.

John Roberts.reasoning: Following our arm-of-the-State framework, the “most important factor” is whether the State treasury is legally exposed to satisfy an adverse judgment, a consideration we emphasized in Hess v. Port Authority Trans-Hudson Corp., 513 U.S. 30, 48 (1994). Here, New Jersey’s statutory structure and financial relationship with NJ Transit indicate substantial State responsibility or exposure for NJ Transit’s liabilities, which strongly supports treating it as an arm of the State for interstate sovereign-immunity purposes. Petitioner’s reliance on the New Jersey Tort Claims Act (N.J. Stat. Ann. §§ 59:1-1 to :12-3) does not supply the clear, express consent required to waive constitutional sovereign immunity, consistent with our insistence on unmistakable waiver and the limits on retrospective monetary liability recognized in Edelman v. Jordan, 415 U.S. 651 (1974). A narrow disposition recognizing immunity on these structural and financial grounds best respects precedent and preserves the States’ dignity interests without attempting to impose a rigid, one-size-fits-all multi-factor test.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Constitution’s structure presupposes state sovereign immunity as an incident of statehood, and that immunity extends to entities that are, in law and practical effect, the State itself. Under this Court’s arm-of-the-State framework, the “most important factor” is whether the State treasury is legally exposed to satisfy an adverse judgment, because that consideration goes to the core impetus for sovereign immunity. Hess v. Port Authority Trans-Hudson Corp., 513 U.S. 30, 48 (1994). New Jersey’s statutory design and fiscal responsibility for NJ Transit’s liabilities point to NJ Transit functioning as an arm of the State, and there is no clear, express waiver of constitutional immunity in the New Jersey Tort Claims Act, which cannot supply constructive consent to suit in sister-state courts absent unmistakable language. Edelman v. Jordan, 415 U.S. 651 (1974).

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Applying the arm-of-the-state framework, the most consequential consideration is the State’s exposure for the entity’s debts and judgments, because sovereign immunity is centrally concerned with protecting the State’s fisc and dignity; Hess identifies the state-treasury risk as the “most important factor” in this inquiry. Where New Jersey’s legal structure makes the State sufficiently responsible for, or exposed to, adverse judgments against NJ Transit, treating NJ Transit as an arm of the State best accords with the Constitution’s immunity principles and avoids the practical consequence of allowing plaintiffs to evade state immunity by suing state instrumentalities in sister-state courts. Petitioner’s reliance on the New Jersey Tort Claims Act (N.J. Stat. Ann. §§ 59:1-1 to :12-3) does not establish waiver of constitutional sovereign immunity, because waiver must be clear and unequivocal, and nothing in that statute amounts to an express consent to suit in other States’ courts. Consistent with Edelman v. Jordan’s insistence on respecting the State’s immunity from monetary liability absent valid consent, I would reject implied or constructive waiver theories premised on “ministerial act” characterizations.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Interstate sovereign immunity should not attach where the entity operates with substantial corporate separateness and functional independence from the State, even if the State may face some fiscal exposure. Under Hess v. Port Authority Trans-Hudson Corp., the state-treasury/judgment-liability factor is important, but it is not invariably dispositive, particularly for public transportation entities that are not uniquely sovereign functions and that States and municipalities alike operate. New Jersey law gives NJ Transit a separate corporate existence and the power to “sue and be sued,” N.J. Stat. Ann. § 27:25-5, and reliance on the New Jersey Tort Claims Act, N.J. Stat. Ann. §§ 59:1-1 to :12-3, cannot supply the “clear, express” consent needed to waive constitutional immunity in another State’s courts. Because treating NJ Transit as an arm of the State here would unduly restrict access to justice for injured individuals without a sufficiently close nexus to core state dignity interests, I would reverse and permit suit.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Under this Court’s arm-of-the-State framework, the “most important factor” is whether an adverse money judgment would, as a practical matter, implicate the State treasury. Hess v. Port Auth. Trans-Hudson Corp., 513 U.S. 30, 48 (1994). If New Jersey’s legal structure makes the State financially responsible or sufficiently exposed to pay NJ Transit’s judgments, that treasury-risk consideration should carry substantial—often dispositive—weight, notwithstanding NJ Transit’s operational separateness and the fact that transit can be provided by non-sovereign entities. Nor does the New Jersey Tort Claims Act (N.J. Stat. Ann. §§ 59:1-1 to :12-3) supply a clear, express waiver of constitutional (interstate) sovereign immunity, which this Court has required rather than implied waiver theories. See Edelman v. Jordan, 415 U.S. 651 (1974).

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Our arm-of-the-State cases treat the State treasury’s legal exposure to an adverse judgment as the “most important factor,” and where state law makes the State formally responsible (or effectively on the hook) for an entity’s liabilities, that strongly indicates the entity shares the State’s sovereign immunity. Hess v. Port Auth. Trans-Hudson Corp., 513 U.S. 30, 48 (1994); see also Edelman v. Jordan, 415 U.S. 651 (1974) (sovereign immunity’s core concern with judgments payable from the public fisc). Whatever NJ Transit’s operational characteristics, if New Jersey’s statutory structure and funding mechanisms render the State ultimately responsible for judgments, that weighs heavily—often dispositively—in favor of treating NJ Transit as an arm of the State. And there is no waiver of constitutional sovereign immunity absent a clear, express statement of consent; nothing in the New Jersey Tort Claims Act (N.J. Stat. Ann. §§ 59:1-1 to :12-3) supplies the sort of unmistakable waiver needed to subject New Jersey or its arm to suit in a sister State’s courts.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Under this Court’s arm-of-the-State precedents, the most important consideration is whether the State treasury is legally responsible (or functionally on the hook) for an adverse judgment, because that financial exposure directly implicates the State’s sovereign dignity and fiscal autonomy. Hess v. Port Authority Trans-Hudson Corp., 513 U.S. 30, 48 (1994), treats treasury liability as the "most important factor," and where New Jersey’s legal structure makes the State sufficiently responsible for NJ Transit’s judgments, that factor should carry substantial—often dispositive—weight notwithstanding NJ Transit’s separate corporate form or operational discretion. Nor is there a valid waiver of constitutional sovereign immunity here: under this Court’s clear-statement approach, statutes like the New Jersey Tort Claims Act (N.J. Stat. Ann. §§ 59:1-1 to :12-3) do not constitute consent to suit in another State’s courts absent unmistakably express language, consistent with the Court’s insistence on express consent rather than implied or constructive waiver. Respect for precedent and practical workability favor a rule that gives primacy to the State’s formal fiscal responsibility to avoid unpredictable, multi-factor balancing that invites interstate friction and undermines the States’ retained immunity.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Under this Court’s arm-of-the-State cases, the “most important factor” is whether the State treasury is legally exposed to an adverse judgment, because that consideration tracks the Eleventh Amendment’s core purpose of protecting state fisc and dignity. Hess v. Port Auth. Trans-Hudson Corp., 513 U.S. 30, 48–49 (1994). Where, as New Jersey argues, state law makes the State formally responsible (or sufficiently on the hook in practical operation) for judgments against NJ Transit, that financial responsibility should carry dispositive or near-dispositive weight even if structural or control indicia are mixed. And absent an unequivocal, express waiver, general provisions of the New Jersey Tort Claims Act (N.J. Stat. Ann. §§ 59:1-1 to :12-3) do not amount to consent to suit in a sister State’s courts, consistent with this Court’s strict waiver principles. See Edelman v. Jordan, 415 U.S. 651 (1974).

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Under Hess v. Port Auth. Trans-Hudson Corp., 513 U.S. 30, 48 (1994), exposure of the state treasury is an important indicator but should not be treated as dispositive where the entity is structured and operates like a separate public enterprise; the arm-of-the-state inquiry also looks to how state law defines the entity and the State’s control over its operations. Edelman v. Jordan, 415 U.S. 651 (1974), underscores that sovereign immunity is meant to protect the State itself from retroactive monetary judgments, which counsels careful attention to functional realities and practical consequences rather than formal budgetary characterizations alone. Given NJ Transit’s operational separateness (as argued by petitioner) and the need for procedural fairness to injured plaintiffs, I would weigh the full set of structural/control factors alongside any asserted judgment-responsibility and conclude NJ Transit has not shown it is the State for interstate-immunity purposes. Nor does the New Jersey Tort Claims Act (N.J. Stat. Ann. §§ 59:1-1 to :12-3) supply the clear, express consent required to waive constitutional immunity, so the case turns on arm-of-the-state status, which on this record I would resolve against immunity.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether New Jersey Transit Corporation qualifies as an “arm of the State” entitled to interstate sovereign immunity, and what weight courts must give to the State’s formal financial liability for judgments when making that arm-of-the-state determination.
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Constitution (state sovereign immunity as reflected in the Eleventh Amendment doctrine and broader structural/constitutional sovereign immunity principles governing suits against States and their arms in other States’ courts); related state-law provisions discussed include the New Jersey Tort Claims Act, N.J. Stat. Ann. §§ 59:1-1 to 59:12-3 (raised in waiver/consent arguments).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Galette (and similarly situated plaintiffs in the parallel New York case) argue that NJ Transit is not an arm of New Jersey for sovereign-immunity purposes because it functions like a public transportation corporation operating with substantial operational and financial independence, and that courts should not treat the State’s potential or formal responsibility for judgments as dispositive—especially where the State has structured the entity to act with corporate attributes and to be sued. Petitioners/Respondents opposing immunity also contend that any claimed waiver/consent issues cannot be resolved by “constructive consent,” but emphasize that New Jersey’s own statutory design and characterization of NJ Transit should weigh against extending sovereign immunity in out-of-state courts.
case_analysis.respondent_position: New Jersey Transit (and New Jersey as supporting respondent in No. 24-1021) contend that NJ Transit is an arm of the State and therefore enjoys interstate sovereign immunity, emphasizing that the State is formally on the hook (directly or functionally) for NJ Transit’s liabilities and that this financial-risk factor should carry special—often controlling—weight. They also argue there has been no clear, unequivocal waiver of immunity for out-of-state suits, and that state tort-claims statutes do not amount to consent to private damages actions in another State’s courts absent explicit waiver, invoking Supreme Court skepticism toward implied/constructive consent.
key_precedents: Infinity Broad. Corp. v. N.J. Meadowlands Comm’n, 901 A.2d 312 (N.J. 2006)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s and Justice Jackson’s fairness concern—that New Jersey should not be able to “corporatize” operations and externalize harms while claiming immunity—has real force, but under our precedent the arm-of-the-State inquiry turns chiefly on whether a judgment is legally or practically one against the State. Hess’s designation of treasury exposure as the “most important factor” is not a mechanical rule, but for a minimalist and administrable approach it should be near-dispositive where, as Justice Kagan emphasizes, state law makes the State the functional backstop for liabilities; otherwise we invite relitigation over formal attributes that States can easily vary. On waiver, Justice Alito is right that a general “sue and be sued” clause and the Tort Claims Act do not supply the unmistakably clear, out-of-state consent Edelman requires, so corporate form cannot do the work of consent by implication. I therefore remain with Respondent on narrow grounds: absent an unequivocal waiver, and given the State’s assumed liability, NJ Transit retains interstate immunity here.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson argue that New Jersey’s choice of corporate form and a “sue-and-be-sued” clause should defeat arm-of-the-State status to prevent States from externalizing harms, but under our sovereign-immunity structure that reasoning conflates policy concerns with the Constitution’s protection of the State’s fisc and dignity. As the Chief Justice and Justice Alito emphasize, Edelman requires an unmistakably clear waiver—especially to be haled into another State’s courts—and generic corporate attributes cannot supply that clear consent by implication. I also agree with Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch that Hess’s identification of treasury exposure as the “most important factor” is not mere administrability; it tracks the core originalist rationale for immunity because a judgment that the State must satisfy is effectively a judgment against the sovereign itself. Corporate formalities and operational latitude therefore cannot override New Jersey’s legal or practical responsibility for judgments absent an explicit out-of-state waiver.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s emphasis on NJ Transit’s corporate form and “sue and be sued” clause is the strongest point for the petitioner, but under our waiver cases that language does not supply the unmistakably clear consent required to subject a State (or its arm) to damages litigation in another State’s courts; as the Chief Justice notes invoking Edelman, waiver must be unequivocal, and generic litigating capacity is not enough. On the antecedent arm-of-the-State question, I agree with Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan that Hess’s identification of state treasury exposure as the “most important factor” has real bite here because the constitutional object of immunity is to prevent judgments that in law or practical effect run against the State fisc. Justice Jackson’s concern about States “externalizing harms” has force as a policy matter, but our methodology does not permit us to treat corporate attributes as overriding where state law makes the State legally or functionally responsible for the entity’s liabilities. Absent an express, out-of-state consent in New Jersey law, allowing sister-state damages suits would invite easy circumvention of interstate sovereign immunity through labeling and form.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s best point is that Hess calls state-treasury exposure the “most important factor,” and they press an administrable, near-dispositive rule when the State is legally or practically on the hook. But Hess’s “most important” language does not, in my view, collapse the arm-of-the-State inquiry into a single-factor test where New Jersey has deliberately created a separately incorporated entity with broad operational powers and an express “sue and be sued” clause—features that matter pragmatically because they shape how the entity interacts with, and can injure, out-of-state individuals. Justice Alito’s reliance on Edelman’s unmistakable-waiver principle does not resolve the antecedent question whether NJ Transit is the State’s alter ego at all; we should not treat ambiguous fiscal backstops as converting a corporatized public carrier into the State itself and thereby foreclosing a forum for injured plaintiffs. A rigid treasury-centered rule risks letting States externalize harms through nominally independent instrumentalities while reclaiming immunity opportunistically, a real-world consequence my methodology cannot ignore.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Jackson and Justice Sotomayor press the best objection: that allowing immunity here lets New Jersey enjoy corporatized, market-facing benefits while shifting the costs of out-of-state harms, and that a “sue-and-be-sued” clause signals real separateness. But Hess’s designation of treasury exposure as the “most important factor” is doing substantive work against precisely that kind of formal toggling, and on this record New Jersey’s legal/functional responsibility for judgments makes NJ Transit look like an alter ego in the way our cases care about. Chief Justice Roberts’s point about Edelman matters because, even if we treat corporate form as relevant, nothing in the Tort Claims Act or the “sue-and-be-sued” language is an unequivocal consent to be haled into another State’s courts for damages—so petitioner’s approach effectively smuggles waiver in through the back door. Pragmatically, giving near-dispositive weight to fisc exposure yields a more administrable and coherent rule than a free-form balancing that would invite relitigation of structural details in every case.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best point is that New Jersey chose a corporate form and included a “sue-and-be-sued” clause, arguably signaling separateness and ordinary litigation exposure. But under our waiver cases, that sort of generic amenability-to-suit language does not supply the “clear, unequivocal” consent to be haled into another State’s courts; as the Chief Justice and Justice Alito stress, Edelman’s clear-statement rule forecloses treating implication or corporate form as an out-of-state waiver. On the antecedent arm-of-the-State question, Hess’s designation of treasury exposure as the “most important factor” cannot be demoted to one factor among many where, as Justice Kagan notes, state law makes the State legally or functionally responsible for judgments—because that is precisely when a judgment operates against the sovereign itself. Petitioner’s holistic approach risks judicial line-drawing untethered from text and precedent, while a fisc-focused rule better fits constitutional structure and administrability.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson press the best point: New Jersey’s choice of separate incorporation plus a “sue and be sued” clause suggests a deliberate move toward market-facing accountability, and we should not let States externalize harms while invoking immunity. But under Hess, as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, the State’s legal or functional responsibility for judgments is the “most important factor,” and giving that factor near-dispositive weight is both precedent-faithful and administrable where (as here) the fisc is effectively implicated. On waiver, I agree with Roberts that Edelman’s unmistakable-clarity requirement is not satisfied by generic “sue and be sued” language or the New Jersey Tort Claims Act absent explicit authorization for out-of-state damages suits; corporate form cannot do the work of an unequivocal interstate waiver. Sotomayor’s functional-independence framing remains relevant at the margin, but it cannot overcome the constitutional concern with judgments that in practical effect run against the State itself.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s and Justice Jackson’s strongest point is that New Jersey deliberately gave NJ Transit separate corporate existence and a “sue-and-be-sued” clause, so we should not let the State enjoy corporatized benefits while invoking immunity. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, Hess identifies state treasury exposure as the “most important factor,” and that focus best fits the constitutional structure interstate immunity protects—preventing judgments that in law or practical effect operate against the State’s fisc and dignity. On the waiver side, Justice Alito is right that Edelman demands unmistakably clear consent, and a general litigation-capacity clause (and the Tort Claims Act’s in-state remedial scheme) does not clearly authorize damages actions in sister-state courts. Corporate form and operational latitude therefore cannot substitute for either (1) the fiscal reality Hess prioritizes or (2) the clear out-of-state consent Edelman requires.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s point that Hess calls treasury exposure the “most important” factor is the hardest for me, because fisc risk is a real sovereign interest; but “most important” is not “categorically dispositive,” and treating it as near-conclusive would let States capture the operational benefits of corporatization while shifting litigation burdens onto injured out-of-state plaintiffs. Justice Thomas and Justice Alito press Edelman’s clear-statement rule, yet that addresses waiver after we decide whether the entity is the State’s alter ego; it cannot be used to collapse the antecedent arm-of-the-State inquiry into a one-factor fisc test. Here, New Jersey’s choice of separate incorporation, broad operational powers, and a “sue and be sued” clause are practical signals of litigating capacity and separateness that, under a fairness- and consequences-aware approach, should prevent automatic exportation of immunity across state lines. Administrability concerns (Justice Kagan) are real, but a holistic Hess analysis is already the Court’s framework, and I do not see a doctrinal basis to elevate ambiguous funding backstops into constitutional immunity absent clearer state-law integration.

John Roberts.reasoning: Our arm-of-the-State cases treat exposure of the state treasury as the central indicator of sovereign immunity, and Hess v. Port Authority Trans-Hudson Corp. identifies whether the State is legally or practically responsible for judgments as the “most important factor.” Given New Jersey’s formal allocation of financial responsibility for NJ Transit’s liabilities, a narrow, precedent-driven resolution would accord dispositive or near-dispositive weight to that factor and treat NJ Transit as an arm of the State for interstate-immunity purposes, absent a clear waiver. Consistent with Edelman v. Jordan, we should require an unequivocal waiver before allowing damages actions that effectively run against the State, and nothing in the New Jersey Tort Claims Act, N.J. Stat. Ann. §§ 59:1-1 to 59:12-3, clearly consents to private suits for damages in other States’ courts. This approach minimizes disruption, respects state dignity, and avoids a broader restructuring of the arm-of-the-state doctrine beyond what our precedents require.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Constitution’s structure, as reflected in the Eleventh Amendment doctrine and this Court’s interstate-sovereign-immunity cases, requires courts to respect a State’s decision to carry out core public functions through entities it creates and controls, absent a clear, unequivocal waiver. In determining whether an entity is an arm of the State, this Court has treated the State’s legal exposure for judgments as the most important indicator because it directly implicates the sovereign’s fiscal and dignitary interests. Under Hess v. Port Authority Trans-Hudson Corp., 513 U.S. 30, 48 (1994), the decisive inquiry is whether the State treasury is legally or functionally liable for adverse judgments, and NJ Transit’s tight statutory integration with New Jersey and the State’s asserted responsibility for its liabilities strongly support arm-of-the-State status. Nor does the New Jersey Tort Claims Act, N.J. Stat. Ann. §§ 59:1-1 to 59:12-3, constitute a clear consent to private damages suits in another State’s courts, and this Court has rejected waiver theories lacking explicit, unequivocal authorization.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Interstate sovereign immunity protects a State and its arms from being haled into another State’s courts absent a clear, unequivocal waiver, and nothing in the New Jersey Tort Claims Act, N.J. Stat. Ann. §§ 59:1-1 to 59:12-3, supplies consent to out-of-state damages suits. In determining whether NJ Transit is an arm of the State, the State-treasury risk carries special—often controlling—weight, because sovereign immunity’s core purpose is to prevent judgments that operate against the State fisc; Hess v. Port Auth. Trans-Hudson Corp., 513 U.S. 30, 48 (1994). Where New Jersey is formally or functionally on the hook for NJ Transit’s liabilities, denying immunity would allow plaintiffs to circumvent the State’s constitutional protection through corporate structuring. Practical consequences also counsel in favor of immunity: exposing a state-run transit entity to out-of-state litigation risks substantial public-funds diversion and interferes with statewide transportation administration.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: NJ Transit’s statutory design and real-world operation point away from treating it as New Jersey itself for purposes of interstate sovereign immunity: New Jersey law gives it a separate corporate existence and the power to “sue and be sued,” and it exercises substantial day-to-day independence rather than acting strictly at the State’s behest. Under Hess v. Port Authority Trans-Hudson Corp., 513 U.S. 30, 45 (1994), operating public transit is not uniquely a core state function, and the arm-of-the-state inquiry must look beyond formal labels to functional and structural realities. While state-treasury risk matters, it should not be treated as dispositive when the State has deliberately structured an entity to operate with corporate attributes and to be subject to suit; otherwise States could externalize harms to injured individuals while invoking immunity whenever convenient. A rule that elevates formal financial liability over these practical indicia would unduly restrict access to justice for injured riders and workers and undermine fairness in cross-border accountability.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Interstate sovereign immunity after Hyatt III extends to States and their arms, so the question is whether NJ Transit is sufficiently state-like under the functional factors this Court has used, including how state law defines the entity, the State’s control, and—critically—the State’s exposure to judgments. Under Hess v. Port Authority Trans-Hudson Corp., the potential impact on the state treasury is the “most important” consideration in the arm-of-the-state inquiry, and where state law makes the State formally or functionally responsible for an entity’s liabilities that factor deserves substantial weight because it directly implicates the core sovereign-immunity concern of protecting the State’s fisc and dignity. The New Jersey Tort Claims Act, N.J. Stat. Ann. §§ 59:1-1 to 59:12-3, does not provide the kind of clear, unequivocal consent required to subject the State (or its arm) to private damages actions in another State’s courts. Balancing workability and coherence, giving treasury liability special weight yields a clearer administrable rule while still leaving room for other structural factors when the fiscal link is genuinely absent.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Our arm-of-the-State inquiry must be tethered to the Constitution’s structure and the States’ retained sovereign immunity, not a freewheeling balancing of “dignity” factors. Under Hess v. Port Authority Trans-Hudson Corp., 513 U.S. 30, 48 (1994), the “most important factor” is whether the State treasury is legally exposed to satisfy an adverse judgment, and courts should give substantial—often controlling—weight to New Jersey’s formal financial responsibility where state law effectively places the State on the hook. New Jersey’s decision to confer corporate attributes (including a “sue and be sued” clause) does not by itself amount to the clear, unequivocal waiver required for suits in another State’s courts, and nothing in the New Jersey Tort Claims Act, N.J. Stat. Ann. §§ 59:1-1 to 59:12-3, clearly consents to out-of-state damages actions. Respect for separation of powers and the Court’s waiver jurisprudence counsels against treating implied or “constructive” consent as sufficient to strip an entity functioning as the State’s instrumentality of interstate sovereign immunity.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Interstate sovereign immunity is a structural constitutional doctrine grounded in the States’ status as coequal sovereigns, and our arm-of-the-State precedents direct courts to give substantial weight to the State’s exposure of its treasury to judgments. Under Hess v. Port Authority Trans-Hudson Corp., the “most important factor” in the arm-of-the-State inquiry is whether the State is legally liable for an adverse damages judgment, and New Jersey’s statutory design and treatment of NJ Transit indicate that the State has assumed (directly or functionally) financial responsibility for NJ Transit’s liabilities. The New Jersey Tort Claims Act, N.J. Stat. Ann. §§ 59:1-1 to 59:12-3, does not provide the clear, unequivocal waiver necessary to subject the State or its arm to private damages suits in another State’s courts. Respect for precedent, state dignity, and workable administration of sovereign immunity thus favors treating NJ Transit as an arm of New Jersey entitled to interstate immunity absent explicit consent.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Interstate sovereign immunity extends to States and their arms absent a clear, unequivocal waiver, and the arm-of-the-State inquiry must give substantial—often decisive—weight to whether the State is legally or functionally responsible for paying judgments. Under Hess v. Port Authority Trans-Hudson Corp., the “most important factor” is state-treasury liability, and the record described here (including New Jersey’s asserted formal fiscal responsibility for NJ Transit’s obligations) places NJ Transit closer to the state-dependent transit entities Hess indicated could enjoy immunity than to the financially independent Port Authority that did not. Nothing in the New Jersey Tort Claims Act, N.J. Stat. Ann. §§ 59:1-1 to 59:12-3, clearly and explicitly consents to private damages suits against NJ Transit in another State’s courts, and Edelman v. Jordan reinforces that sovereign-immunity waivers must be unmistakably expressed rather than implied. Given that framework, NJ Transit qualifies as an arm of New Jersey for purposes of interstate sovereign immunity on these facts.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: I would hold that New Jersey Transit Corporation is not an arm of the State for purposes of interstate sovereign immunity because the inquiry must be holistic and focused on practical realities, not dominated by a formal or contingent treasury-risk label. Under Hess v. Port Authority Trans-Hudson Corp., 513 U.S. 30, 48-49 (1994), the state-treasury factor is “most important” but not dispositive where, as here, state law gives NJ Transit a separate corporate existence and broad operational powers, including the ability to “sue and be sued,” and public transit is not a uniquely sovereign function. Giving controlling weight to New Jersey’s asserted formal responsibility for judgments would elevate form over function and undermine procedural fairness for out-of-state plaintiffs when the State has structured the entity to operate with corporate attributes. Nor does the New Jersey Tort Claims Act, N.J. Stat. Ann. §§ 59:1-1 to 59:12-3, amount to the kind of clear, unequivocal consent required to extend immunity (or waiver) to private damages suits in another State’s courts.
